title: Many agents on purpose

story: Nova's diff for a bigger ticket touches 14 files. One reviewer misses things on a diff that size, so we want several: one looking for bugs, one for security, one for weak tests, and for every important finding a skeptic that tries to prove it wrong. That is easily ten agents.

If Nova starts them one by one through the Agent tool, every report lands in Nova's own context, and Nova spends its turns deciding what to start next. And someone on the team asks the natural question: if ten reviewers are good, why not ten agents writing the code in parallel too?
hook.question: How do I run many agents in a planned shape, and how do I decide when more agents help and when they hurt?

read.h: Move the plan into a script
p: A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that starts many subagents and holds the plan itself: the loops, the fan-out, what to keep and what to drop. A runtime inside Claude Code runs the script in the background, and the session that started it gets back only the script's final return value. In the panel below, three lenses (a lens is one reviewer agent told to look for one kind of problem) each read a big diff, and the session sees one short list of findings.

This changes who decides. With subagents, the model decides turn by turn what to start next, and every result passes through its context. With a workflow, the script decides, and the intermediate results live in script variables. That makes the orchestration something you can read, save, rerun and test, like any other code.

More agents help with reading, searching, reviewing and comparing plans, because those jobs are independent and their results can be merged. They hurt with writing code: two agents editing the same repo at once produce conflicts. So the rule for our agents is many readers, one writer.

notes.text: meta comes first and must be a plain object literal: no variables, no function calls.
A hand-written JSON Schema. Scripts cannot import zod or anything else.
phase() groups the agents that follow in the progress view.
parallel() takes functions and runs them at the same time; each starts one agent.
An agent that was stopped or failed returns null, so drop those before reading .findings.
One skeptic per important finding, all in parallel.
Only this value goes back to the session that started the workflow.

p: The body is plain JavaScript with top-level await, and a few globals. agent(prompt, options) starts one subagent and resolves to its text, or to an object when you pass a schema; it resolves to null when the agent was stopped or hit an error it could not recover from. parallel() runs a list of functions at once and waits for all of them. pipeline(items, stage1, stage2) sends each item through the stages on its own, with no waiting between items, so the security lens's skeptics can start while the tests lens is still reading. phase() and log() feed the progress view, and args is whatever input the caller passed.

A script cannot import modules or touch the file system; the agents do that work. Date.now(), Math.random() and new Date() without arguments throw inside a script. That is on purpose: a stopped run can be relaunched in the same session, and completed agents with an unchanged prompt return their saved result instead of running again, which only works if the script builds the same prompts every time.

Because the script is just JavaScript, you can test its logic without any model. The lab gives you a stand-in runtime with fake agents that answer from a JSON file, so you can see the order of agents, the null handling and the final result in a second.
read.see:
phase Lenses
  agent  1  correctness            -> answered
  agent  2  security               -> answered
  agent  3  tests                  -> null
phase Skeptics
  agent  4  src/cart.ts:42         -> answered
  agent  5  src/api.ts:12          -> answered
log   1 of 2 important findings survived

read.h: Start it from a session, sized on purpose
p: In the SDK, a workflow starts through the built-in Workflow tool. In a dontAsk session the tool must be approved like any other, with Workflow in allowedTools, or Workflow(<name>) for one saved workflow. Saved workflows live in .claude/workflows/ in the project or ~/.claude/workflows/ in your home folder, and run by the name in their meta.

The agents a workflow starts use the session's permission rules, so starting the panel from a read-only session keeps every lens and skeptic read-only. Three numbers bound a run. CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENTS sets how many agents run at the same moment; the default is 16, fewer on a machine with fewer CPUs. The runtime stops a run at 1,000 agents and refuses a parallel() or pipeline() list longer than 4,096 items. The workflowSizeGuideline setting (small means fewer than 5 agents) is advice to the model that writes a script, not a limit.

notes.text: A read-only session plus the Workflow tool: the workflow's agents cannot edit anything.
Under dontAsk the Workflow tool must be approved, or the launch is refused.
Advice for scripts the model writes. It does not cap a saved script.
At most three agents at the same moment, as on a small machine. The others wait their turn.
modelUsage counts the workflow's agents too, so the cost of the whole panel is here.

deeper.h: Go deeper: relaunching a stopped run
p: The Workflow tool's result carries a runId. If a run is stopped, calling Workflow again with resumeFromRunId replays it in the same session: completed agents whose prompt and options are unchanged return their saved result, and the first changed or failed agent runs again, with every agent that started after it.
This works only inside the same session, which is one more reason to resume the session itself after a crash, as in the previous lesson.

lab.title: A review panel, tested without a model
needs: For the last step only: your own Anthropic API key with access to dynamic workflows
lab.goal: Write a workflow script, run its logic with a stand-in runtime and fake agents, break and fix its null handling, then launch it from a read-only session.

guess.q: A workflow starts three lens agents with parallel(). The tests lens is stopped halfway. What does parallel() give back for it?

options.text: The partial findings it had so far
options.why: A stopped agent returns nothing partial to the script.

options.text: null, in that agent's place in the list
options.why: agent() resolves to null for a stopped or failed agent, so scripts filter with .filter(Boolean).

options.text: Nothing: parallel() throws and the whole run fails
options.why: Inside parallel() and pipeline() the run carries the null and goes on. Only an agent you await directly can end the run with its error.

follow.say: Save the panel from the Understand step as a project workflow.
follow.do:
cd ~/sdk-lab && mkdir -p .claude/workflows
# write .claude/workflows/review-panel.js from the Understand step

follow.say: Write the stand-in runtime. It gives the script fake versions of agent(), parallel(), pipeline(), phase() and log(); each fake agent answers from a JSON file by its label, and a missing answer behaves like a stopped agent.
Give the fake agents their answers: two lenses with findings, no answer for the tests lens, and a verdict from each skeptic.
follow.do:
cat > answers.json <<'EOF'
{
  "correctness": { "findings": [
    { "path": "src/cart.ts", "line": 42, "severity": "important", "body": "total ignores the discount when the cart has one item" },
    { "path": "src/cart.ts", "line": 7, "severity": "nit", "body": "rename t to total" } ] },
  "security": { "findings": [
    { "path": "src/api.ts", "line": 12, "severity": "important", "body": "user id is read from the query string" } ] },
  "src/cart.ts:42": { "refuted": false },
  "src/api.ts:12": { "refuted": true }
}
EOF
npx tsx src/dry-run.ts .claude/workflows/review-panel.js answers.json '{"diffPath":"/tmp/diff.patch"}'
follow.see:
phase Lenses
  agent  1  correctness            -> answered
  agent  2  security               -> answered
  agent  3  tests                  -> null
phase Skeptics
  …
log   1 of 2 important findings survived
result {"findings":[{"path":"src/cart.ts","line":42,…}]}  (5 agents)

sed 's/found.filter(Boolean).flatMap/found.flatMap/' .claude/workflows/review-panel.js > broken-panel.js
npx tsx src/dry-run.ts broken-panel.js answers.json '{"diffPath":"/tmp/diff.patch"}'
follow.see:
agent  3  tests                  -> null
<anonymous_script>:19
const important = found.flatMap((r) => r.findings).filter((f) => f.severity === 'important')
                                         ^
TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'findings')

follow.say: Now the real runtime. Put any small diff into diff.patch, write src/run-panel.ts from the Understand step, and run it with your key.
follow.do:
git diff --no-index /dev/null src/kb.ts > diff.patch
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...   # your own key
npx tsx src/run-panel.ts
follow.see: (Needs your key and workflow access; numbers and findings differ.) One cost line per model in modelUsage, including the agents the workflow started, then the session's summary of the findings that survived.

lab.build: Rewrite the panel with pipeline() instead of two parallel() rounds, so each lens's skeptics start as soon as that lens is done instead of waiting for all three lenses. pipeline(LENSES, stage1, stage2) passes each lens's result into stage 2, which starts one skeptic per important finding and returns the finding or null. Flatten the results at the end and drop the nulls. Your dry run must give the same result as before: one finding, src/cart.ts:42, from five agents.
checks: The dry run of review-panel.js prints two phases, five agents and one surviving finding.
Without .filter(Boolean), the dry run stops with TypeError: Cannot read properties of null.
Your pipeline() version prints the same result line from five agents.
With your key, modelUsage lists more than one cost line, because the workflow's agents are counted.
lab.fix: A teammate wants a big refactor done faster and writes a workflow that starts six agents with parallel(), each told to "update the imports in your part of src/". They run it from Nova's normal session, which has Edit and Write. Half the files now have broken imports, and two agents edited the same index.ts. Explain what went wrong with this shape, and rewrite it as many readers and one writer: agents that each return a list of needed changes, and a single agent (or Nova itself) that applies them.
explain: What does a workflow script hold that a session with subagents keeps in the model's context instead?
Why do Date.now() and Math.random() throw inside a script?
Why are parallel reviewers safe and parallel writers not, and what makes the panel's agents read-only?
lab.done: Your panel's logic is tested with fake agents, survives a stopped agent, and runs from a read-only session.

check.q: When does a workflow help more than one agent working alone?

options.text: When many independent reads or reviews can run at once and be merged into one short answer
options.why: Readers and reviewers do not interfere with each other, and only the merged result enters the session's context.

options.text: When the code change is large, so several agents can write parts of it at once
options.why: Parallel writers edit the same repo and conflict. Our rule is many readers, one writer.

options.text: Whenever the ticket is urgent, because more agents always finish sooner
options.why: More agents cost more tokens and add merging work. They pay off only for independent work.

check.q: Why does Math.random() throw inside a workflow script?

options.text: Because scripts run in a browser sandbox without Math
options.why: Math exists; only the calls that make runs differ are blocked.

options.text: So that a relaunched run builds the same prompts and can reuse the saved results of finished agents
options.why: Replay matches agents by prompt and options. A random value or the current time would change them every run.
It has nothing to do with memory. It is about replaying a run the same way.

check.q: A session with dontAsk has allowedTools: ["Read", "Grep", "Glob"] and is asked to run a saved workflow. What happens?

options.text: The workflow runs, because saved workflows are always trusted
options.why: In the SDK the launch goes through the normal permission checks like any tool call.

options.text: The workflow runs, but its agents may not use any tools
options.why: The launch itself is the problem: it is never approved.

options.text: The Workflow call is refused, because the tool is not approved
options.why: Add Workflow, or Workflow(<name>) for one saved workflow, to allowedTools.

p: Nova uses two saved workflows, baked into the VM user's ~/.claude/workflows/. nova-research runs four helpers in parallel before planning (where the code is, similar past PRs, which tests cover the area, what the brain says) and, for a fuzzy ticket, three plans from different angles plus a judge that picks one. nova-review-panel runs five lenses on a bigger diff and a skeptic per important finding, and it is started from the read-only reviewer session, so none of its agents can edit.

Nova decides when a workflow is worth it, guided by one line in its planning skill; the harness never forces one. The harness sets CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_MAX_CONCURRENT_AGENTS by VM size (3, 6 or 12), and Workflow is in Nova's allowedTools so the launch passes under dontAsk. A spike first checks that workflows run headless in a VM behind the gateway.

tickets.why: The spike: run a saved workflow headless in a VM, check concurrency, cost counting and resume.
nova-research.js: parallel research helpers, three plans and a judge for fuzzy tickets.
nova-review-panel.js: lenses, then skeptics, from the read-only reviewer session.

words.plain: A JavaScript script, run by a runtime in Claude Code, that starts many subagents and holds the plan itself.
Starts one subagent from a script; resolves to its text, an object with a schema, or null.
Runs a list of functions at the same time and waits for all of them.
Sends each item through a chain of stages on its own, with no waiting between items.
The built-in tool that starts a workflow from a session; under dontAsk it must be approved.

review.q: Name the globals a workflow script can use and one thing it cannot do.
review.a: agent, parallel, pipeline, phase, log and args. It cannot import modules or use the file system, and Date.now(), Math.random() and new Date() throw.

review.q: What makes the review panel's agents unable to edit files?
review.a: It is started from a read-only session, and a workflow's agents use that session's permission rules.

remember: A workflow moves the plan into a script: many readers in parallel, one writer, and only the final answer comes back.
